Get started with bootmakr in R

Source: vignettes/bootmakr.Rmd
bootmakr.Rmd

A regression coefficient from observational data is only as credible as the assumption that no important variable was left out. sensemakr (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020) makes that assumption concrete: it reports the coefficient you would have obtained had a variable as strong as one of your observed covariates been omitted. bootmakr adds a standard error, a confidence interval and a p-value for that adjusted coefficient, obtained by resampling the data the way you would choose standard errors for the regression itself. This is needed because the usual tools, the impact threshold of a confounding variable (ITCV) and the analytic interval of sensemakr, break down when the regression calls for robust standard errors (Lonati & Wulff, 2026); Why bootstrap? shows why. This page shows a first analysis from start to finish. The same steps in Stata are in Get started in Stata.

Installation

bootmakr is installed from GitHub. sensemakr, which it builds on, comes from CRAN and is installed along with it.

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jespernwulff/bootmakr")

The example data

The package comes with firms, a simulated panel of 250 firms observed for 20 years. Because the data are simulated, we know the truth: the effect of x on y is 0.25. Two firm-level characteristics affect both x and y, an observed control c and a variable q that we pretend not to have. The within-firm components of x and of the disturbance are persistent, so standard errors must be clustered by firm. (The data are a variant of the simulated example in Lonati and Wulff, 2026; see ?firms for how they were generated.)

library(bootmakr)
data("firms")
head(firms)
#>   firm year         y         x          c         q
#> 1    1    1 1.1135241 0.7462263 -0.3820026 0.6451423
#> 2    1    2 0.5718906 0.5223299 -0.3820026 0.6451423
#> 3    1    3 0.6579784 0.8940660 -0.3820026 0.6451423
#> 4    1    4 1.2859237 1.2648760 -0.3820026 0.6451423
#> 5    1    5 1.3447777 1.2004796 -0.3820026 0.6451423
#> 6    1    6 0.8935023 0.8371407 -0.3820026 0.6451423

Here is the regression a researcher without q would run.

coef(lm(y ~ x + c, data = firms))["x"]
#>         x 
#> 0.4445283

The coefficient is 0.44 instead of 0.25, because q drives both x and y. With real data you would not know this. What you can ask is how the result would change if a variable as strong as something you do observe had been left out. That is the question bootmakr answers.

A first analysis

sensemakr needs a benchmark: an observed covariate that sets the scale for the omitted variable. We take c and ask what the coefficient of x would be had a variable as strong as c been omitted. In these data that is exactly what q is.

first <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                  benchmark_covariates = "c",
                  cluster = "firm",
                  seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
first
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x", benchmark_covariates = "c", 
#>     seed = 123, cluster = "firm", progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 5,000, 250 clusters)
#> Benchmark: c | kd = 1, ky = 1
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>   Estimate Std. Err     2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)  
#> x 0.252134 0.076236 0.087365 0.394215     0.01 *
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                       Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> c with treatment | X      0.1433       0.379
#> c with outcome | D, X     0.1248       0.353
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>           kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx Impact
#> 1.00x c 1.00 1.00 0.1673  0.1998  0.222
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates. Impact: product of
#>  its partial correlations with the outcome and with the treatment, both given the
#>  covariates only, i.e. the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable
#>  biases the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the variance
#>  estimator, and not a threshold.)

The call names the model, the treatment (treat), the benchmark (benchmark_covariates) and, because observations of the same firm are not independent, the variable that identifies the clusters to resample (cluster). Everything else is left at its default: an omitted variable exactly as strong as the benchmark (kd = 1) and 1,000 bootstrap replications. seed makes the result reproducible, and progress = FALSE switches off the progress bar, which is useful on screen but not in a document. The run takes about 15 seconds.

Reading the output

The adjusted estimate. Had a variable as strong as c been omitted, the coefficient of x would be 0.252 rather than 0.445. This is the estimate sensemakr reports for the same benchmark, and it is close to the true 0.25. It does not involve the bootstrap.

Its uncertainty. The remaining columns come from the bootstrap. In each of the 1,000 replications bootmakr draws firms with replacement, refits the regression and recomputes the adjusted estimate. The standard deviation of those 1,000 values is the standard error (0.076), their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form the 95 percent confidence interval (0.087 to 0.394), and the p-value (.010) is twice the smaller of the two shares of replications that fall on either side of zero. The effect of x remains positive and statistically distinguishable from zero even if an omitted variable as strong as c is at work.

The benchmark strength. The last block says what “as strong as c” means. c explains 14.3 percent of the variance of x and 12.5 percent of the variance of y that x leaves unexplained. The omitted variable this implies has an impact of .22: the product of its partial correlations with y and with x, which is the scale on which the ITCV is stated. All of this is computed from the data. No standard error is involved, so the block is the same whatever variance estimator you prefer. See How strong is the benchmark? for the details.

From one strength to many: the breakdown point

An omitted variable as strong as c does not overturn the result. How much stronger would it have to be? Give kd several values and bootmakr evaluates each of them on the same bootstrap samples.

sweep <- bootmakr(y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x",
                  benchmark_covariates = "c",
                  kd = seq(0.5, 1.5, by = 0.25),
                  cluster = "firm",
                  seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
sweep
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = y ~ x + c, data = firms, treat = "x", benchmark_covariates = "c", 
#>     kd = seq(0.5, 1.5, by = 0.25), seed = 123, cluster = "firm", 
#>     progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps, n = 5,000, 250 clusters)
#> Benchmark: c | kd = 0.5 0.75 1 1.25 1.5, ky = 0.5 0.75 1 1.25 1.5
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (percentile 95% CI):
#>             Estimate Std. Err      2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)    
#> x (kd=0.5)  0.354042 0.052479  0.253451 0.456146        0 ***
#> x (kd=0.75) 0.304696 0.062805  0.176416 0.425069        0 ***
#> x (kd=1)    0.252134 0.076236  0.087365 0.394215     0.01   *
#> x (kd=1.25) 0.195903 0.093321 -0.013573 0.363798    0.066   .
#> x (kd=1.5)  0.135458 0.115036 -0.126653 0.328123    0.276    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; CI and p-value from percentile bootstrap)
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                       Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> c with treatment | X      0.1433       0.379
#> c with outcome | D, X     0.1248       0.353
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>           kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx Impact
#> 0.50x c 0.50 0.50 0.0836  0.0973  0.113
#> 0.75x c 0.75 0.75 0.1255  0.1478  0.168
#> 1.00x c 1.00 1.00 0.1673  0.1998  0.222
#> 1.25x c 1.25 1.25 0.2091  0.2536  0.274
#> 1.50x c 1.50 1.50 0.2509  0.3093  0.324
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates. Impact: product of
#>  its partial correlations with the outcome and with the treatment, both given the
#>  covariates only, i.e. the scale of the ITCV; signed so that the omitted variable
#>  biases the estimate away from zero. Descriptive only: independent of the variance
#>  estimator, and not a threshold.)
plot(sweep, type = "kd_sweep")
Adjusted estimate and bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval for an omitted variable 0.5 to 1.5 times as strong as c. Solid markers: p < .05.

The adjusted estimate shrinks as the assumed omitted variable grows stronger, and its confidence interval widens. In this run the result holds up to an omitted variable 1 times as strong as c and breaks down at 1.25 times: from there on the interval includes zero. That breakdown point is a compact summary of how robust the finding is. (A p-value printed as 0 means that none of the 1,000 replications fell on the other side of zero.)

Checking the answer

Simulated data have one advantage over real ones: the omitted variable is in the file. The regression that includes q gives

coef(lm(y ~ x + c + q, data = firms))["x"]
#>         x 
#> 0.2286068

which lies inside the bootstrap interval at kd = 1. The Why bootstrap? article uses the same data to show what the ITCV and the analytic interval of sensemakr make of this example.

Working with the results

The object returned by bootmakr() keeps everything that was computed.

sweep$results
#>     kd  estimate         se    ci_lower  ci_upper pvalue     r2dz.x    r2yz.dx
#> 1 0.50 0.3540423 0.05247928  0.25345109 0.4561464  0.000 0.08363943 0.09728672
#> 2 0.75 0.3046965 0.06280549  0.17641581 0.4250691  0.000 0.12545914 0.14781734
#> 3 1.00 0.2521337 0.07623598  0.08736489 0.3942151  0.010 0.16727885 0.19983870
#> 4 1.25 0.1959030 0.09332121 -0.01357331 0.3637976  0.066 0.20909857 0.25356964
#> 5 1.50 0.1354581 0.11503646 -0.12665311 0.3281231  0.276 0.25091828 0.30927622
#>      impact
#> 1 0.1134982
#> 2 0.1682740
#> 3 0.2216809
#> 4 0.2736747
#> 5 0.3242071

estimate to pvalue are the columns of the printed table. r2dz.x and r2yz.dx are the partial R2 values of the omitted variable assumed in each row, and impact its impact. The benchmark-strength block is stored as a list.

first$benchmark_strength
#> $type
#> [1] "single"
#> 
#> $observed
#>   benchmark   r2dxj.x  r2yxj.dx   r_dxj.x  r_yxj.dx
#> 1         c 0.1433067 0.1247742 0.3785587 0.3532339
#> 
#> $implied
#>   benchmark kd ky    r2dz.x   r2yz.dx    r_dz.x   r_yz.dx    r_yz.x    impact
#> 1         c  1  1 0.1672789 0.1998387 0.4089974 0.4470332 0.5420107 0.2216809
#> 
#> $r_yd.x
#> [1] 0.4201003

The bootstrap draws themselves are in $boot_samples, one column per value of kd, so the distribution can be inspected without rerunning anything.

quantile(first$boot_samples[, 1], c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>       2.5%        50%      97.5% 
#> 0.08736489 0.24821315 0.39421508

plot(first, type = "histogram")
Bootstrap distribution of the adjusted estimate at kd = 1. The dashed line marks the estimate in the original sample.

Finally, $sensemakr_orig holds the sensemakr object of the original fit, so everything sensemakr offers (its summary, robustness values and contour plots) remains one step away.

The choices you make

The benchmark. Choose an observed covariate that is strong and that you can argue an omitted variable is unlikely to exceed. Report why you chose it. A group of covariates can serve as a joint benchmark with gbenchmark_covariates = c("x1", "x2").

The multiple. kd scales the benchmark’s relationship with the treatment and ky its relationship with the outcome. ky follows kd unless you set it.

The resampling scheme. It should mirror how the data were sampled and how you would compute standard errors in the regression itself. Without cluster, rows are resampled, which allows for heteroskedasticity. With cluster = "id", whole clusters are resampled. cluster = c("id1", "id2") requests two-way clustering, and strata a stratified bootstrap. See Clustered and stratified data.

Replications and seed. The default of 1,000 replications is fine for a first look. For results you report, use more (5,000 or 10,000), set a seed, and when the verdict is close to the significance threshold check that it has settled with the converge argument.

Where next

  • The worked example takes a published study through a complete analysis: the choice of standard errors, the benchmark, the breakdown point, a grouped benchmark and the convergence check.
  • Why bootstrap? shows, on these data, why the ITCV and the analytic interval of sensemakr cannot be trusted with robust standard errors.
  • ?bootmakr documents every argument, ?plot.bootmakr the three plots, and ?firms the data.
  • The Stata command of the same name runs the same analysis. See R and Stata side by side.
